379.title: Chaupai close
379.hook: a short prayer for the times you feel unsafe
379.tomorrow: Anand Sahib: the song of bliss
379.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Chaupai Sahib in the morning Nitnem and within the evening Rehras, and many also say it at night, before travel or in times of fear; Kirtan Sohila is the bani usually said before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last couplet, and your line, your door. Did the doorways catch you? Today, the whole Chaupai, and where to keep it. Day three hundred seventy-nine.

It's late. The lights are off, and the house has gone quiet, and that's exactly when the mind gets loud. The thing someone said at work. The test results that aren't back. The noise outside that's probably nothing. Night has a way of making every worry bigger. Some people turn on a podcast. Some scroll. Many Sikhs, for generations, have done something else at that hour. They say a short prayer they know by heart. And the one many reach for in the dark is the one you've spent ten days with. Today: Chaupai close.
screen: `LATE, LIGHTS OFF, MIND LOUD.` → `NIGHT MAKES WORRY BIGGER.` → `A PRAYER KNOWN BY HEART.`

segments.voice: Lay the prayer out end to end. A humble request, benti, in four-part verse. Protect me, giving me your hand. May my heart's wish be fulfilled, and my mind rest at your feet. End the enemies, outside, and for many Sikhs, inside: the five thieves. Carry my servants and Sikhs across the river. Then the prayer looks up: the Creator spreads creation out and gathers it in, knows every heart, and recognizes the pain of the good and the bad. Then, since I held your feet, I look to no one else. And at last, leaving every other door, I have come to yours; Gobind is your servant. Ten days, one prayer, one movement. Keep me. That's the whole of it, in two words. Where does it live in a Sikh day? In the morning, as one of the five banis of the Nitnem. In the evening, inside Rehras, the prayer said at dusk. At the amrit ceremony, stirred into the water. And, for a great many Sikhs, in all the unscheduled moments too: before a long drive, at a hospital bedside, on a plane, in the dark. Ahead on this path, you'll meet Kirtan Sohila, the bani many Sikhs say last thing at night before sleep. Chaupai isn't a replacement for that. It's more like the pocket prayer, the one that fits in the gaps. It's short, it's personal, it asks for the most basic thing there is. And it was written by someone who knew real danger, so it never pretends danger isn't real. It just asks, in the middle of it, to be kept.
screen: `HAND, HEART, ENEMIES, THE RIVER.` · `SPREADS, GATHERS, KNOWS THE PAIN.` · `THE FEET, THEN THE DOOR.` · `MORNING, DUSK, AND THE GAPS.` · then, large: `KEEP ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep it for night-time. Right now, in daylight, choose the line from Chaupai you want for the dark. Maybe the hand. Maybe the heart's wish. Maybe he knows the pain, or every other door. Say it slowly a few times, in the original if you can, in English if you can't, until it starts to feel familiar. Breathe between repetitions. If you pray, you can join it to Waheguru. Tonight, when the lights go off and the mind gets loud, that line is waiting for you. The bell holds the time.
Chaupai close. Ten days of one prayer, the hand, the heart's wish, the enemies, the river, the knower of hearts, the feet and the door, folded into two words: keep me.
Your line: keep me. Tonight, when you turn the light off, say your chosen line once before anything else. Day three hundred seventy-nine.

screen: `DAY 379 COUNTS.` → `CHAUPAI, DONE.` → `TOMORROW: ANAND SAHIB: THE SONG OF BLISS.`

380.title: Anand Sahib: the song of bliss
380.hook: forty pauris of joy found through the Guru, closing every Sikh gathering
380.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite all forty pauris of Anand Sahib in the morning Nitnem, and the first five pauris with the fortieth are sung at the close of nearly every Sikh service and ceremony, before the Ardas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chaupai closed, and your line was keep me. Did your night-time line come back to you? Now a new bani begins, the one Sikhs sing together. Day three hundred eighty.

At a Sikh wedding, the couple walks slowly around the Guru Granth Sahib four times while the four verses called the Laavan are sung. Then the music shifts. Before the final prayer, the whole room joins in a song: grandparents, cousins, friends who flew in, kids who've been fidgeting for an hour. The same song closes the ordinary Sunday service, a baby's naming, and a funeral. And the wedding itself shares its first word: the ceremony is called Anand Karaj, the ceremony of bliss. Today, the bliss: Anand Sahib.
screen: `FOUR ROUNDS, THE LAAVAN SUNG.` → `THEN THE WHOLE ROOM SINGS.` → `ANAND KARAJ: THE CEREMONY OF BLISS.`

segments.voice: Anand means bliss, a deep, settled joy. Anand Sahib is a bani by Guru Amar Das, the third Guru, written in Raag Ramkali and set in the Guru Granth Sahib: forty pauris, forty stanzas. You first met it on day one hundred thirty-three. Now we'll walk through it slowly, the way we walked through the Japji and Chaupai. Two forms of it matter. Many Sikhs say all forty pauris in the morning, as one of the five banis of the Nitnem. And a short form, the first five pauris and the last, six in all, closes nearly every Sikh gathering, followed by the Ardas. Sikh tradition tells a story about its beginning. Guru Amar Das, it's said, composed it when a grandson was born to his family, and the child was given the name Anand. Whether or not every detail is exact, the story fits. This is a song that comes out of a family's joy. And that's the angle for today: together. Anand Sahib isn't usually a solo. It's the song a room sings. A wedding sings it on the way into a marriage. A funeral sings it on the way through grief. The same words, in both rooms. That says something about what anand means in this tradition. It isn't the high of a good day. It's a joy deep enough to be sung beside a coffin as well as beside a bride. A joy that can hold sorrow without breaking. And it's found, the song will say, through the Guru. Over the coming days we'll take it pauri by pauri. Today, just the sound of a room singing.
screen: `ANAND: DEEP, SETTLED JOY.` · `FORTY PAURIS; SIX CLOSE EVERY GATHERING.` · `BORN, TRADITION SAYS, OF A FAMILY'S JOY.` · `SUNG AT WEDDINGS AND FUNERALS ALIKE.` · then, large: `BLISS, TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to the six ceremony pauris. If you can, find a recording of the short Anand Sahib, the six pauris sung at the close of a Sikh service, and let it play. It takes only a few minutes. Don't worry about understanding the words yet. Just listen to the sound of many voices singing one thing. Breathe slowly with it. If you can't play it now, picture a room full of people you love singing together, and hold that picture. If you pray, you can join with Waheguru at the end. The bell holds the time.
Anand. Bliss, a deep and settled joy; Guru Amar Das's forty-pauri song, whose six pauris close nearly every Sikh gathering, weddings and funerals alike.
Your line: bliss, together. Today, share one good moment with someone instead of keeping it to yourself, and notice how joy grows when it's shared. Day three hundred eighty.

381.title: Pauri 1, sound: anand bhaiaa
381.hook: anand bhaiaa meree maae satguroo mai paaiaa
381.howItsDone: Many Sikhs learn the opening of Anand Sahib by ear in childhood, singing it at the close of services; in kirtan it is sung in Raag Ramkali or in simpler congregational tunes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anand, the song of bliss, and your line, bliss, together. Did you share one good moment with someone? Today, the very first line, just its sound. Day three hundred eighty-one.

You know how a song can get into you before you understand a word of it. A lullaby in a language you don't speak. A chant at a stadium. The first bars of a tune your grandmother hummed in the kitchen. The sound arrives first, and the meaning catches up later, sometimes years later. Plenty of Sikh kids can sing the opening of Anand Sahib long before anyone explains it to them. The sound has carried it. So today, before we open up a single word of meaning, we'll just learn how it sounds. Today: Pauri 1, sound: anand bhaiaa.
screen: `A SONG GETS IN BEFORE THE WORDS.` → `SOUND FIRST, MEANING LATER.` → `TODAY, JUST THE SOUND.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line, transliterated: anand bhaiaa meree maae satguroo mai paaiaa. Let's walk through its sounds. Anand, with the stress on the second syllable: a-NUND. Bhaiaa: bha-I-aa, three soft beats, it means has happened, has come. Meree maae: MAY-ree MAA-ay, my mother, a call, the way you'd call out to someone in the next room. Then satguroo: sat-GU-roo, the True Guru. Mai: me, I. Paaiaa: PAA-i-aa, have found. Notice the music in it. Bhaiaa at the middle, paaiaa at the end. The line rhymes with itself, and the long aa sounds keep opening, like a mouth that's singing rather than speaking. That's on purpose. This is written in a raag, Ramkali, and it's meant to be sung. Now listen to how the pauri ends. Its last line comes back almost to the start: kahai Naanak anand hoaa, satguroo mai paaiaa. Says Nanak, bliss has come; I have found the True Guru. The circle closes on the sound it opened with. Every pauri of Anand Sahib ends with kahai Naanak, says Nanak. And here's a detail worth knowing. Guru Amar Das wrote this, not Guru Nanak. But in the Guru Granth Sahib, the Gurus who wrote after Guru Nanak sign their verses with his name. The Granth marks which Guru wrote what with a number, Mahala three for Guru Amar Das, but the name in the verse is always Nanak. Sikhs understand that as one light passing from Guru to Guru. So when you say this line, you're saying words of the third Guru, signed with the name of the first.
screen: `A-NUND BHA-I-AA MAY-REE MAA-AY.` · `BHAIAA AND PAAIAA: IT RHYMES.` · `EVERY PAURI ENDS: KAHAI NAANAK.` · `THE THIRD GURU SIGNS AS NANAK.` · then, large: `ANAND BHAIAA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say the first line aloud. Sit comfortably. Breathe in, and on the out-breath say it slowly: anand bhaiaa meree maae satguroo mai paaiaa. Don't worry about getting it perfect. Say it again, a little slower, letting the long aa sounds open. Then once more, and this time, if you like, let it tip into a tune, any tune. If you'd rather, just say the first two words, anand bhaiaa, over and over, softly. If you pray, you can follow it with Waheguru. Then sit in the quiet after the sound. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 1. The opening of Anand Sahib, learned by sound: anand bhaiaa meree maae, satguroo mai paaiaa, with every pauri ending kahai Naanak.
Your line: anand bhaiaa. Today, hum or whisper those two words once, anywhere, the kitchen, the car, the stairs, and let the sound do the work. Day three hundred eighty-one.

382.title: Pauri 1, meaning: joy, mother
382.hook: joy, mother, I have found the True Guru, easily, and the songs of joy are sung (Anand 1)
382.tomorrow: Stay with the Lord, my mind
382.howItsDone: The first pauri of Anand Sahib is sung at the close of nearly every Sikh gathering, from weddings to ordinary services, and is often the part of the bani Sikhs know best by heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of pauri one, and your line, anand bhaiaa. Did you hum it somewhere ordinary? Today, the same pauri, opened up for its meaning. Day three hundred eighty-two.

A baby is born in a Punjabi family, and within the hour the phone is ringing. Then the doorbell. Aunties arrive with sweets. Uncles arrive with more sweets. Someone puts music on. Everyone keeps saying one word to the parents, the grandparents, anyone standing still long enough: vadhaiyan! Congratulations! It's the word for good news so big that the whole family turns up. The first pauri of Anand Sahib has that word in it. It's a party in five lines, and the guests are not who you'd expect. Today: Pauri 1, meaning: joy, mother.
screen: `A BABY IS BORN; THE PHONE RINGS.` → `AUNTIES, SWEETS, MUSIC.` → `VADHAIYAN! CONGRATULATIONS!`

segments.voice: Here's the pauri, in paraphrase. Joy has come, my mother, for I have found the True Guru. I found the True Guru with ease, and my mind rings with congratulations. The jewel-like ragas, with their families, have come to sing the Word. Sing the Word of the Lord, all you who have set it in your minds. Says Nanak, bliss has come; I have found the True Guru. Take the pieces. First, mother. The news goes to the person you'd tell first. Then sahaj, with ease. The Guru wasn't won by force. Sahaj is a big word in Sikh thought: a natural, settled ease, the opposite of straining. The joy didn't come from clawing. It came the way sleep comes. Then the party. Vaadhaaeeaa, congratulations, the same word aunties call out at a birth. And who shows up to celebrate? The ragas. In Indian music, ragas are often pictured as having families, consorts and companions. So the pauri pictures the musical modes themselves arriving at the door like relatives, ready to sing. It's a wonderful image: joy so big the music turns up in person. Then, a turn outward. Sing the Word, all of you who've taken it in. The joy doesn't stay private. It's an invitation to everyone else in the room. And finally, back to the beginning: bliss has come. Notice what this whole pauri is not. It isn't a lecture about joy. It's a report of joy, from inside it, still breathless. That's what Guru Amar Das gives Sikhs to sing at the end of every gathering: not an idea about bliss, but good news.
screen: `JOY HAS COME, MY MOTHER.` · `SAHAJ: FOUND WITH EASE.` · `THE RAGAS ARRIVE LIKE FAMILY.` · `SING THE WORD, ALL OF YOU.` · then, large: `JOY, MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share one good news. Sit and breathe slowly first. Let your mind go over the last few days and find one piece of good news, any size. A friend's recovery. A finished project. A good conversation. A small win nobody noticed. Let yourself feel it again, the way the pauri does, from inside. Then, when the bell ends, tell someone. Call your mother, or whoever you'd tell first. Send the message. Let the joy go out the door instead of staying in. If you pray, you can thank the Guru with Waheguru first. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 1, meaning. Joy has come, my mother: the Guru found with ease, the mind ringing with congratulations, and the ragas arriving like family to sing.
Your line: joy, mother. Today, when good news comes, yours or someone else's, say congratulations out loud and mean it, the way family does. Day three hundred eighty-two.

383.title: Stay with the Lord, my mind
383.hook: ae man meriaa too sadaa rahu har naale: stay always with the Lord and your troubles will pass (Anand 2)
383.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this second pauri as part of the short Anand Sahib sung at the close of services, and the opening line is often quoted as a reminder to keep the mind with God through the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the meaning of Pauri 1, and your line, joy, mother. Did you share some good news? Today, pauri two, where the Guru talks to his own mind. Day three hundred eighty-three.

Do you talk to yourself? Most people do, even if they'd never admit it. Come on. Focus. Don't check the phone. You've got this. Some of it is harsh, the inner voice that sounds like a bad coach. Some of it is kinder. Either way, the mind needs reminding, again and again, of what it already knows, because it wanders off the moment you stop watching it. The second pauri of Anand Sahib is the Guru talking to his own mind. Not to a crowd. Not even to God, exactly. To himself. Today: stay with the Lord, my mind.
screen: `EVERYONE TALKS TO THEMSELVES.` → `THE MIND NEEDS REMINDING.` → `THE GURU TALKS TO HIS OWN MIND.`

segments.voice: The pauri opens, transliterated: ae man meriaa too sadaa rahu har naale. O my mind, always stay with the Lord. Man is the mind, the restless inner self. Meriaa: my. Sadaa: always. Har naale: with the Lord, alongside. Then, in paraphrase: stay with the Lord, my mind, and all your pains will be forgotten. He will take you as his own, and set all your affairs right. The Master can do all things; why forget him from your mind? And it ends where it began: says Nanak, my mind, always stay with the Lord. Notice the tone. It's not scolding. It's the voice of someone who has just found joy in pauri one, turning to his own wandering mind and saying, stay. Don't drift off now. Naale is a lovely little word. It's beside, alongside, the word you'd use for walking with a friend. Not under. Not far above. With. And notice the promise is about the pains being forgotten, not about them never happening. The troubles are real. Staying beside the Lord is what loosens their grip. Angeekaar, the word for being taken as his own, is the same idea you met in Chaupai: being claimed, held, adopted. And then that gentle question: why forget him? Not a threat. Almost puzzled. If the Master can do everything, why would you wander off? It's the question you'd ask a child who keeps letting go of your hand in a crowd. That's the second pauri. The joy has come. Now the work is to stay with it.
screen: `AE MAN MERIAA: O MY MIND.` · `NAALE: ALONGSIDE, LIKE A FRIEND.` · `THE PAINS FORGOTTEN, NOT ABSENT.` · `WHY FORGET HIM? NOT A THREAT.` · then, large: `STAY WITH HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay with one thing. For the next two minutes, choose one simple thing to stay with: your breath, a candle, the sound of a fan, a word like Waheguru if you pray. Every time your mind wanders off, and it will, gently bring it back, the way the pauri does. No scolding. Just: stay. Count how many times you return, if that helps. Then, later today, try it for five whole minutes with something ordinary: washing dishes, a walk, a cup of tea. Stay with that one thing the whole way through. The bell holds the time.
Stay with the Lord. Ae man meriaa too sadaa rahu har naale: the Guru telling his own mind, gently, to stay beside the Lord, and the pains will loosen.
Your line: stay with him. Today, whenever you notice your mind has wandered off, say to it, kindly, the way you'd talk to a friend: stay. Day three hundred eighty-three.

384.title: What your house doesn't hold
384.hook: true Master, what is there that is not in Your house (Anand, opening pauris)
384.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this third pauri as part of the short Anand Sahib sung at the close of every service, and its opening question is often quoted as an expression of trust and contentment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pauri two, and your line, stay with him. Did your mind wander, and did you bring it back? Today, pauri three asks a question about a house. Day three hundred eighty-four.

Some homes have a pantry that never seems to run out. You've maybe been in one. A grandmother's kitchen where, no matter how many people turn up, there's always more: another pot of dal, another stack of rotis, a box of sweets from somewhere. You arrive hungry and you leave carrying leftovers. You never once wonder whether there'll be enough. Pauri three of Anand Sahib asks a question about a house like that, except the house is God's, and the question is almost a laugh of wonder. Today: what your house doesn't hold.
screen: `A KITCHEN THAT NEVER RUNS OUT.` → `YOU LEAVE WITH LEFTOVERS.` → `A QUESTION ABOUT GOD'S HOUSE.`

segments.voice: It opens like this, in paraphrase: O true Master, what is there that is not in your house? Then: everything is in your house. In the original, the opening is saachiaa saahibaa, kiaa naahee ghar terai. True Master, what isn't in your home? It's a question that answers itself. Then the pauri says that the one who keeps your praise always, and holds your Name in their mind, finds the music of the Word playing within. And it closes by asking the question again: says Nanak, true Master, what is not in your house? Now, two things make this more than a nice sentiment. First, the word ghar, house or home. In Sikh scripture, ghar often means more than a building. It's the inner home too, the self, the heart, where the Guru teaches that the One is found. So the question works on two floors. Nothing is missing from God's house. And, the pauri hints, nothing is missing from the house within you, either, if the Name is living there. Second, look at who this is for. Most of us live with a quiet feeling of lack. Not enough time, money, love, energy, success. Advertising depends on it. Pauri three meets that feeling with a question. What is missing? Not, here's what you should want. Just: look around the house. What isn't here? The pauri also says something we'll stay with in a few days: that each person receives what the Master gives. For today, just the wonder. The house is full. Nothing is missing.
screen: `TRUE MASTER, WHAT ISN'T IN YOUR HOUSE?` · `GHAR: HOUSE, AND THE HOME WITHIN.` · `THE QUIET FEELING OF LACK.` · `LOOK AROUND: WHAT IS MISSING?` · then, large: `NOTHING IS MISSING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: list what you already have. Sit and breathe slowly. Then, in your head or on paper, start a list of what's already in your house. Not just things. A roof. Water from a tap. A person who'd answer if you called. Your two hands. A memory you love. Today. Keep going until the list surprises you a little, until it's longer than you thought it would be. If you pray, you can say Waheguru after each one, or at the end. If you don't, just let the size of the list sink in. The bell holds the time.
What your house doesn't hold. Pauri three: true Master, what is not in your house? Everything is there, and the same may be true of the home within.
screen: `WHAT YOUR HOUSE DOESN'T HOLD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: nothing is missing. Today, when you feel the pinch of not enough, ask yourself the pauri's question, what is missing, and actually look. Day three hundred eighty-four.

pairs: the music of the Word within

in Sikh scripture, ghar only ever means a building
it often means the inner home too: the heart, where the One is found.
the pauri tells the listener exactly what to want

trapdoor: what you thought: a line about God being rich.
what it means: a question that answers itself, nothing is missing from the Master's house, and maybe not from the home within.
what a scholar hears: ghar in gurbani often means the inner self as well as a dwelling, so 'kiaa naahee ghar terai' works on both levels, God's house and the heart where the Name lives.

385.title: The Name my support
385.hook: the true Name is my support and satisfies every hunger (Anand, opening pauris)
385.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this fourth pauri as part of the short Anand Sahib at the close of services, and many remember the Name, saying Waheguru or a short prayer, before eating.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pauri three, and your line, nothing is missing. This week: Chaupai closed with keep me, Anand began, bliss together, anand bhaiaa, joy mother, stay with him, nothing is missing. Today, pauri four. Day three hundred eighty-five.

Ever eaten a whole meal and still felt hungry? Not stomach hungry. The other kind. You finish dinner and find yourself opening the fridge again, or scrolling for something to buy, or reaching for a phone that has nothing new on it. There's a hunger that food doesn't touch. Most of us feed it all day long with whatever's nearest, and it never quite fills. The fourth pauri of Anand Sahib names something it says does fill that hunger, all of it. It uses a word that also means the thing a building stands on. Today: the Name my support.
screen: `A WHOLE MEAL, STILL HUNGRY.` → `THE FRIDGE, THE SCROLL, THE PHONE.` → `A HUNGER FOOD DOESN'T TOUCH.`

segments.voice: The pauri begins and ends with one line, transliterated: saachaa naam meraa aadhaaro. The true Name is my support. Aadhaar means support, foundation, the base a thing rests on. The same word, as it happens, names India's national identity number today: the foundation record. In the pauri it's the ground under your feet. Then, in paraphrase: the true Name is my support; it has taken away all my hunger. It brought peace and calm to live in my mind, and fulfilled all my longings. I am forever a sacrifice to the Guru, who gives such greatness. Says Nanak, listen, saints: love the Word. The true Name is my support. Three things to notice. First, hunger. Bhukh, the word for it, is the plain everyday word, the hunger you'd feel before lunch. The pauri says the Name takes away all of it. It's a bold claim, and it's made from experience, not as a theory. Second, the order. First support, then hunger gone, then peace comes to live in the mind. Peace isn't chased. It moves in, once the foundation is there. Third, the sacrifice. Kurbaan, to give yourself wholly, the word people use when they'd do anything for someone. The joy of the first three pauris turns into gratitude here, so full it wants to give itself away. And it ends by asking the listener, gently, to love the Word too. Notice that the pauri doesn't tell you to stop eating, or stop wanting. It describes what happens when the deepest hunger is met. The smaller hungers lose their power. You're fed underneath.
screen: `AADHAAR: SUPPORT, FOUNDATION.` · `THE NAME TAKES AWAY ALL HUNGER.` · `THEN PEACE MOVES INTO THE MIND.` · `KURBAAN: GRATITUDE THAT GIVES ITSELF.` · then, large: `MY SUPPORT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: eat slowly, satisfied. If you have something to eat nearby, a piece of fruit, a cracker, even a sip of tea, take it now. If not, keep this for your next meal. Take one bite and stop. Taste it fully. Chew slowly. Notice the moment your body says, that's good. Breathe between bites. Let yourself be satisfied by a little. If you pray, you can say Waheguru before the first bite, the way many Sikhs remember the Name before eating. If you don't, just let the bite be enough. The bell holds the time.
The Name my support. Saachaa naam meraa aadhaaro: the true Name is my foundation, and it takes away all hunger, so peace can come and live in the mind.
Your line: my support. Today, at one meal, eat the first few bites slowly, and see if being satisfied comes sooner than you thought. Day three hundred eighty-five.

original.note: Gurmukhi: aadhaar, support or foundation; in pauri four, the true Name is my support.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pious line about God being important.
what it means: the true Name as the foundation you stand on, which meets the deepest hunger, so peace can move in.
what a scholar hears: aadhaar, from Sanskrit for that which holds up, is paired with bhukh, the plain word for hunger, and the pauri is framed by its own refrain, a common shape in Anand.
